newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Vranitzky pushed to head ECB - paper.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Vranitzky pushed to head ECB - paper.

text.p: Austria's ruling Social Democrats have launched a clandestine campaign for ex-chancellor Franz Vranitzky, who resigned last month, to head the future European Central Bank (ECB), daily Die Presse reported on Friday.
"Behind the scenes, there are attempts to make the former chancellor the head of the European Central Bank," the paper said without naming its sources.
Austria was one of the most recent entrants to the European Monetary System (EMS), seen as a precursor to Europe's single currency which is slated to be phased in from January 1999.
The Alpine republic joined the EMS in January 1995, and is widely believed to be among the firmest candidates for early membership of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).

If rumours become reality, Vranitzky would be up against hefty competition. Dutch central bank chief Wim Duisenberg earlier this month officially announced he was in the running for the post of ECB head.
There have also been reports of a French candidate for the post, but Germany's powerful Bundesbank was reported to have thrown its weight behind Duisenberg.
The ECB will evolve from the European Monetary Institute, scheduled to be chaired by Duisenberg, in 1999 after nations adopt the single currency, the euro.

Vranitzky, widely known in Austria as the "pinstriped Socialist", resigned from his job at the helm of Austria's government and the country's Social Democrats on January 18, hinting he had become tired with politics.

Observers said one of his key achievements during his 10-year tenure was to lead Austria from the fringes of western Europe into the heart of the European Union, which it joined in 1995 after more than two-thirds of Austrians voted in favour of membership in a referendum in June 1994.
Vranitzky, Europe's second longest-serving leader after German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, was replaced by Viktor Klima, then finance minister.
At the time of his surprise resignation, the soft-spoken Vranitzky denied he had any ambitions to take up a post in the European political arena. -- Knut Engelmann, Vienna newsroom +431 53112 274
